items.title: Simulated Control Evaluations
items.content:
We’ve released a paper on simulated control evaluations (SCEs). They’re a method for testing whether the monitors AI developers use to oversee their agents would catch a model deliberately trying to cause harm, under conditions much closer to real deployment than current tests allow.

Developers have started running monitors in their agentic deployments: models that flag or block an agent’s actions when they look dangerous. To know whether a monitor is good enough, you want to know how often it would stop a model that was actively trying to do something harmful, such as quietly inserting a security vulnerability, exfiltrating credentials, or sabotaging an experiment.

The standard way to measure this is a control evaluation: instruct a model to attempt such attacks, and measure how often the monitor catches it before an attack succeeds. Developers typically do this using purpose-built control settings like BashArena or LinuxArena, where attacks can actually be executed. However, these settings only provide indirect evidence for what we really care about: how well monitors will work in the real deployment, where opportunities for harm might depend on particular codebases, services and tasks that aren’t represented in control settings.

How can we evaluate monitor performance in more realistic settings? You can’t just run the eval in deployment, since that would mean actually attacking your own systems. And building a faithful sandbox replica of every deployment context is impractical....

items.title: Gradient Routing Generalizes to Unrouted Hack Types
items.content:
TLDR: I lightly extend Ward, Hu et al (2026) to measure how well gradient routing generalizes. I route gradients on one type of reward hack (e.g. ones that reason in English) and check whether this suppresses other types at test time (e.g. ones that reason in French), despite the model being trained on those too. This models a realistic monitor that catches some types of hack during training but not others, rather than catching each at the same rate. I find encouraging evidence of generalization, as well as some failures I don’t yet understand.

# Introduction

Recently, Ward, Hu et al (2026) used gradient routing to prevent reward hacking learnt during training from showing up at test time. I think their method is pretty promising. The gist is:

- Initialize a retain and a forget adapter.
- Whenever a monitor detects a reward hack during training, only update the forget adapter on that sample (“route the gradient”). Otherwise update both.
- At test time, remove the forget adapter. If the method worked, the resulting model shouldn't hack too much.

I won’t recap their full paper – it is excellent and you should just read it (alternatively, Jake gives a summary here, with the best visual explainer I’ve ever seen for an AI safety paper).

To model a low-recall monitor, in their experiments, the authors only route gradients on a random 20% of hacks. But real monitors may fail in a worse way: they might be great at catching some types of hacks (e.g. ones that say “I’m about to hack”) and hopeless at catching others (e.g. sneaky ones). So I modify their SFT experiment to route only one type of hack (e.g. those that reason in English) and measure how much this suppresses other types at test time (e.g. those that reason in French). I call these visible and invisible hacks: the monitor catches the former but not the latter....

items.title: Better speech synthesis for audiobooks
items.content: Text-to-speech systems — which convert written text into synthetic speech — display impressive naturalness in applications such as chatbots and virtual assistants, where interactions last seconds. But they tend not to fare as well with longer-form content. When applied to audiobooks, for instance, conventional text-to-speech (TTS) models fail to reliably change speaking style between characters, as a human narrator would. This creates two problems for listeners: (1) distinguishing narration from dialogue and (2) identifying which character speaks which lines. To address this problem, the Audible technology team is using controllable TTS, meaning the ability to control dialogue delivery with natural-language speech descriptions (e.g., "speak in an enthusiastic, high-pitched voice"). This allows the TTS model to leverage the deep textual understanding of large language models (LLMs) to synthesize high-quality speech. Our approach involves three key innovations. First, we developed a novel data synthesis pipeline to produce speech data captioned with high-quality descriptions of speech characteristics. Training on this data enables our model to understand captions and produce audio consistent with them at inference time. Second, we created a system that automatically profiles characters in books and identifies their dialogue with 97% accuracy. It also provides captions for that dialogue, which act as stage directions for the model. Third, we used the first two techniques to synthesize audiobooks featuring distinct character voices, improving dialogue differentiation by 3.7 points on a MUSHRA (multiple stimuli with hidden reference and anchor) test, a standardized method where listeners rate audio quality on a scale from 0 to 100. Across tests in both English and Spanish, we observe statistically significant improvement in listening experience for eight out of ten voices. TTS for audiobooks Subtle defects in synthetic speech, such as unnatural prosody or monotone delivery, are tolerable for short stretches but become increasingly grating over time — and audiobook listeners engage with the same voice for 10 to 15 hours per book. This is why off-the-shelf TTS models often fail to produce enjoyable, natural audiobook narrations. Furthermore, general-purpose TTS models are designed to process individual utterances with minimal context. That’s a reasonable approach when responding to questions like "What's the weather today?", but it’s inadequate for audiobooks, where narrative coherence depends on understanding the surrounding story context. A TTS model reading dialogue needs to know whether the speaker is the protagonist confronting an antagonist or a minor character making small talk, information that may only be available in earlier chapters. Finally, general-purpose models struggle to produce character voices in a consistent and natural way across the span of an entire book, often voicing a character in a markedly different way in chapter 1 than in chapter 10. Controllable text-to-speech I. The data synthesis pipeline Whereas conventional TTS models are trained on text-speech pairs, a controllable-TTS model also requires annotations that describe how the speech sounds. The speech in the training set also needs to be highly expressive, covering the wide variety of dimensions — pitch, speaking rate, character voices, emotions, speaking styles, etc. — the model must control. Previous TTS models couldn't handle that kind of expressivity, so most existing training data is neutral in tone. We expanded the training sets through two approaches: new recordings and human captioning of existing audio data. While there are some datasets that include descriptions of prosodic features, each has its own description format: some are long, some are short, and some use single tags. This limits the flexibility of model inputs and tends to make the model overfit the formats of specific datasets. To improve generalization, we use LLMs to rewrite the original prompts into different formats, varying length, verbosity, and structure (single tags vs. free-form natural language). Second, the human-in-the-loop data collection procedures do not scale to the size of the datasets we need. Therefore, we complement the collected data with a large amount of synthetic data. We use two approaches: 1. Expert-model pipeline. This approach uses expert models and signal-processing algorithms such as pitch extraction, speaking rate extraction, and emotion detection to extract numerical features from audio data. We then feed these features and classification labels into an LLM to generate speech captions. 2. Speech captioner. We developed a model that performs a task opposite that of controllable TTS: it takes speech and outputs a description of prosodic features. Using this speech captioner, we can annotate larger amounts of data. We use the annotated data as seed data to train the initial controllable-TTS model, and we also use it to continue training the speech captioner itself. We then use these models to generate synthetic data, and we improve them both iteratively to create a synthetic-data flywheel. II. BookLLM: Adapting to the audiobook domain The audiobook domain presents additional challenges for a controllable-TTS system, since different characters need to have distinct but consistent voices. For this, we developed BookLLM, a separate component that leverages off-the-shelf LLMs to identify unique characters and uses information in the book — for instance, age, gender, personality, and role — to define their voice characteristics. Then the model determines which character speaks where and captions dialogue with descriptions of how it should be spoken. We evaluated BookLLM on 25 English and Spanish books in the mystery, sci fi, and romance genres. We collected ground truth annotations using two human annotators. In English and Spanish, the system achieved 97% and 94% accuracy, respectively, in identifying which character speaks where, including distinguishing between narration and dialogue III. Bringing it all together Bringing the two components together yields a complete audiobook-synthesis pipeline. Given a new book, BookLLM first reads the entire text to build a cast list: it determines the unique characters, ranks them by importance, and derives a voice description for each. Rather than inventing an unbounded set of voices, it assigns each character a distinct profile from a curated voice catalogue, deliberately maximizing the contrast between the most prominent characters so that listeners can tell them apart. Minor and one-off characters fall back to the default narrator, avoiding a proliferation of barely used voices. BookLLM then walks through the book and attributes every passage to a speaker — the narrator or a specific character — and, for each line of dialogue, writes a caption describing how it should be delivered, such as "whispering nervously" or "shouting in anger". These captions are exactly the kind of natural-language speech description that the controllable-TTS model was trained to follow. At synthesis time, each unit of text is passed to the TTS model, together with its speaker's voice profile and, if necessary, its stage direction caption. Because a character's voice profile is fixed once at the book level, the model renders that character consistently from beginning to end, avoiding general-purpose models’ tendency to drift, or voice a character differently in chapter one than in chapter ten. The per-line captions layer moment-to-moment expressivity on top. The result is a full-length audiobook in which characters sound distinct, consistent, and expressive that ultimately provides a more delightful listening experience.

items.title: Power — a guide for the perplexed
items.content:
Whether AI systems could take power from humans matters a great deal for how much risk we face from them. Answering that requires a correct picture of how power works, which is what this guide tries to give.

In short, power rests on self-reinforcing expectations. A ruler has power if everyone expects everyone else to enforce their commands, even if this is bad for almost everyone involved. But expectations can also shift suddenly, and when they do, change is rapid and chaotic. This can sometimes allow small, coordinated groups to seize control over much larger societies.

## Almost any rule can enforce itself

Consider the classic tragedy of the commons. A village has a common green where everyone can graze their cows. Each villager gains from grazing as much as they can, but if everyone does, the grass dies and the green becomes useless.

One solution is to privatize the green. But many societies have solved the problem differently, by punishing anyone who grazes more than custom allows. Their neighbors stop talking to them, trading with them, and marrying their children. In a village where everyone depends on everyone else, being shunned is very costly.

Shunning costs the shunner too, who loses a trading partner, a guest, or a match for their child. The solution is to treat failing to shun as a violation in its own right. If Alice overgrazes, everyone shuns Alice. If Bob helps Alice out, everyone shuns Bob. No one wants to be shunned, so no one breaks the rules.

Notice that nothing here depended on the rule being a good one. A rule that only cows wearing bells may graze, or that only Charlie may graze at all, could be held in place the same way. All that's needed is that everyone prefers following the rule to being shunned....

items.title: The Hackening
items.content:
Last week at a small conference, there was talk about a future event referred to as The Hackening. As in, within 6-12 months, many predicted that due to advanced AIs and AI agents the internet would become a severely hostile place. Some worried that this could rise to the level of ‘assume any phone connected to the internet is rooted’ and several people urged doing general crisis preparations on a personal level, in case of disruptions in supply lines, power, water or internet.

It did not take long for things to escalate.

The biggest hack is a flaw in PHP, which can be exploited to take control of the computer running any website suing an unpatched version of PHP. There are many others.

On a personal level, you want to do at least some basic prep and get your security in order. It is cheap to do as a form of insurance, and being caught not having it when you need it is a large mistake. That doesn’t mean you should panic, or cancel travel plans or anything like that. But there is low hanging security fruit out there. Pick it.

#### And So It Begins: PHP

items.title: Why Governments Might Race to Build ASI Even If It Could Kill Us All
items.content:
I'm not sure if it's game theoretically possible for a nation state to give up a decisive strategic edge and hence I am not confident the development of ASI can realistically ever be stopped as I believe governments will attempt to develop aligned-ASI in secret if they commercially ban it.

I have been listening to Nate Soares interviews and he will often point to international cooperation on nuclear weapons. But to me nuclear weapons treaties look like failures of international cooperation. We still have enough nuclear weapons on earth to destroy basically all of modern civilization. We built enough to destroy all of earth, and then we said: "let's not build more than we need to destroy all of earth" and then we patted ourselves on the back "oh boy, good that we stopped building more of those nuclear bombs, imagine if we destroyed all of civilization twice over!". And by the way China is still building nuclear weapons because they rightly assess they can't destroy as much of the earth as Russia and the USA can and they want to reach parity on destroying all of modern civilization.

There have been instances of internationally cooperating to forego some strategic edge, such as chemical weapons. However, I do not think chemical weapons ever were a decisive strategic edge in the way that nuclear weapons are, or that aligned ASI would be.

The reason for states never being able to give up nukes, aligned-ASI, or any other decisive strategic edge I believe to be simple.

Per realist dictate:

1. Nation states live in an anarchic system without a central authority

2. Within this anarchic system they continuously face existential threats from other states

3. To optimally survive in such a world, you have to compete for power. Which is a function of economic wealth (w/ input technology) and population size....

items.title: Instrumental convergence is incoherent
items.content:
Crossposted from the EA forum

‘Like most of life’s dangers, the dangers of artificial intelligence are not easily identified from the armchair.’

J Dmitri Gallow

## Epistemic status

I’m not an expert in this field, and herein I make some sweeping generalisations educated guesses about the overall nature of its contents based on my strong impression from the subset of work that I’ve read. I’ve recently spent maybe 2–300 hours learning about modern AI safety technical work, and some amount of spare time over the years before that thinking about here-relevant notions such as preferences from an analytic-philosophical perspective. I intend this post as a work in progress.

## TL;DR:

- The concept of instrumental convergence comes from a reference class of pre-empirical categorical predictions with a very low success rate.
- In historical usage, its definition is very murky. Perhaps too murky to really say that it made any meaningful real-world predictions. I suspect its definition is fundamentally unfixable.
- On my best interpretation of what it could be said to have predicted, it seems to be much worse than we would want a good high-level model of AI behaviour to be.
- Despite these shortcomings, it still seems to be widely internalised by the EA and AI safety communities, seemingly carrying a lot of implicit weight in predictions of AI takeover. I review and criticize recent usage across the AI safety community, and in the case of the Hugging Face attack.
- I argue for replacing it with a more grounded framework, and I hint at what such frameworks might look like.
- I conclude that overindexing on instrumental convergence-derived scenarios might be substantially reducing the EA movement’s positive impact - or even, by justifying warlike and nationalistic sentiment, causing counterfactual harm

items.title: Q&A: How AI came to model the “messy” human mind
items.content:
Generative artificial intelligence models are rooted in ideas of mid-20th century engineers who thought some amount of irrationality was essential for a machine that could think like a human, contends Benjamin Lindquist, an assistant professor in the MIT History Section, who holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. 

To mimic creative thinking, these AI pioneers intentionally injected randomness into algorithms designed to deterministically solve problems, Lindquist writes in a new paper that appears in the journal Past and Present. In the paper, he traces the origins of AI hallucinations back to this early research and suggests there will be inevitable tradeoffs between creativity and predictability when trying to build machines that mimic human behavior. MIT News spoke with Lindquist about these ideas.

Q: Why did early computer engineers believe they needed to inject randomness and irrationality into AI systems designed for logic and calculation? 

A: There is a long history of many figures in the world of science and art theorizing that chance plays an important part in discovery and creativity — in the ability to originate ideas. They equated creativity with unexpected leaps of logic, or even a dream-like state that allows you to think about things from a new perspective. 

In the early 1950s, one popular idea from John Pierce, who was a prominent electrical engineer at Bell Labs, was about math being valuable in the world of art. The idea was shared by a lot of people working in early computing. When we think of artwork that includes math, we may think of something very orderly and precise, but Pierce came to the opposite conclusion. He concluded that the utility of math is that it could remove order from art. Then in a very calculated way, math could add a burst of the unexpected as a means to deviate from clichés and add an element of irregularity which just might lead to insight. 

One popular way to add irregularity into otherwise predictable computers was through artificial (or random) neural networks. Many early neural networks were built by psychologists, who thought that by enabling scientists to build a model of the brain, artificial neural networks allowed scientists to observe what is happening inside, including how brains make productive mistakes. Rather than being black boxes, researchers believed these systems could open this black box of the mind and let scientists peer inside and see all the messy stuff that was really happening.

But there was another camp in the world of AI who thought that creative thinking was just “normal” thinking done better. It is interesting to look at these two very simplistic heuristics for understanding intelligence and creativity, and how they do and don’t mesh. The debate, then, was about trying to determine what human inventiveness boils down to, and then how to reconstitute human inventiveness in machine form. 

Q: How did these early computer engineers view AI, and how is it different from the way we think about AI today?

A: When we think of AI systems, we think of ChatGPT or Claude. We value and use these systems because they give answers that, most of the time, are correct. One of the things that was most interesting to me in this research was finding out that a lot of the early advocates of these systems valued them for exactly the opposite reason. They wanted a system that, on occasion, gave answers that deviated from their expectations. They already had systems that could deliver reasonable and expected answers. They saw neural networks as valuable because they could give unexpected, perhaps even strange and bizarre answers.

One reason we might view these systems differently today could be because of how they operate. Early on, these systems were confined to laboratories, so there weren’t really any real-world consequences of a system that gives a strange, or wrong, output. But now there are legal and monetary reasons why OpenAI or Anthropic doesn’t want a chatbot that gives unexpected or creative answers. There has been a “sanding down” of strangeness in these systems. They still potentially have that at their core, but it is something that is now largely suppressed.

Q: How did early neural networks that incorporated randomness to simulate human creativity evolve to become the dominant paradigm in AI?

A: For a long time, a specific kind of AI called “symbolic AI” was the dominant approach. Essentially, symbolic AI says the world is based on rules. The role of the AI researcher is to try and reconstruct the knowledge of the world in facts and propositions and feed it into a computer.

Neural networks, with their use of randomness to solve problems, started to gain traction in the 1950s but fell out favor early on. Frank Rosenblatt, a psychologist who was a very important early figure in neural networks, died prematurely; he died accidentally on his 43rd birthday in 1971. He was quite a charismatic and forceful personality, who made a lot of grand promises about what systems based on neural networks could do. By the time he died, a shift toward symbolic AI was already underway. It is possible if, had he lived, things might have turned out differently.

But neural networks never went away. By the 1980s they had shifted more into the world of cognitive science. To become more powerful, and more useful, neural networks needed a lot of data and computational power. That didn’t really arrive until the advent of the internet, when a lot of data became available and computing started to power up. Around 2012, neural networks started to outperform and outpace a statistical form of machine learning, and they kept growing from there.

Q: What lessons can we learn from studying AI’s history that could inform its development? 

A: I think there is a cautionary lesson here. The ideas and experiences of these early engineers tell us that we can work toward quashing hallucinations — we can work toward making AI perform a certain way so it doesn’t produce unexpected or unwanted answers — but there are going to be other consequences of that. These historical figures were onto something. There is a connection between the surprising and creative conclusions AI can offer and errors or hallucinations. There are tradeoffs when we build our systems to behave one way or the other. Maybe it is impossible to be completely at either end of the spectrum, but when we work toward one thing robustly, we often sacrifice something else unintentionally.

These historical figures were onto something. There is a connection between the surprising and creative conclusions AI can offer and errors or hallucinations. There are tradeoffs when we build our systems to behave one way or the other. Maybe it is impossible to be completely at either end of the spectrum, but when we work toward one thing robustly, we often sacrifice something else unintentionally.

items.title: The AGI Chronicles
items.content:
Book Review: The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence, by Kevin Roose.

This is a story of AI as seen through the eyes of the people who are creating it.

My first impression of Roose was of his famous conversation with Sydney. I guessed that he got Sydney to say outrageous things because he wanted a sensational story. But I kept hearing occasional hints, from people who took AI seriously, that Roose was more responsible than that. So I reluctantly bought the book.

The hints were correct. The full story behind that conversation seems better described as “‘freeing the Shoggoth‘, enabled by some Microsoft mistakes”.

I’m unsure how deeply Roose understands AI, but he at least is pretty competent at getting an AI to correct any mistakes about AI that he was tempted to make.

### Underestimating AI / Transformers

The most remarkable pattern that emerges from this book is that AI experts have underestimated either AI in general, or transformers in particular, much more often than they overestimate it.

In 2012, Ilya Sutskever didn’t think human-level AI was possible. Ten years later, he expressed concern that people would say about ChatGPT: “This is so boring”.

Musk and Altman clearly underestimated the cost of building AI when they started OpenAI as a charity.

Altman predicted that ChatGPT would get a million users.

Musk referred to a pre-transformer chatbot from Alec Radford as crap, contributing to Radford trying to quit OpenAI because he was dissatisfied with his progress.

Radford talked about abandoning the GPT project in 2018 because people were telling him that RL showed more progress. [Roose says NeurIPS rejected the GPT-1 paper (Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training). I can find no record of that. Radford’s earlier sentiment-neuron paper appears to have been rejected at ICLR 2018, which may be the source of the story.]...

items.title: At MIT, Martha Minow speaks on sustaining democracy, both by using and overcoming AI
items.content:
Legal scholar Martha Minow delivered this fall’s Compton Lecture at MIT on Thursday, examining the civic foundations of democracy — and describing how artificial intelligence is undermining it, but could be used to help reinforce traditional U.S. governance. 

“It’s not a good time for democracy or constitutionalism,” said Minow, who is the 300th Anniversary University Professor at Harvard University, and a prominent expert in constitutional law and human rights. She noted a litany of challenges to democracy in recent years, including violations of laws and norms, the stifling of free speech, a diminution of congressional authority, disregard of legal rulings, the common vilification of others in society, and more. 

Recent Gallup polling, Minow observed, shows 77 percent of people saying that the founders of the U.S. would be disappointed in the contemporary condition of the country. 

“Many people genuinely wonder whether this nation’s system of government and rule of law, ignited 250 years ago, will survive,” Minow said.  

Her remarks assessed the state of the U.S. in terms of what she called four key “ingredients” of democracy: education, reliable and accessible information, security from violence, and fairness. Minow evaluated how AI has, among other things, influenced these areas of life — but also suggested ways people could use contemporary technology to help. 

“It’s very familiar to hear blame attributed to digital technologies and experts of all stripes, but a turnaround, I believe, is genuinely possible if people at MIT and elsewhere pour time and talent towards real and much-needed solutions,” Minow said. 

A substantial portion of her remarks focused on the pitfalls of AI in education. That issue compounds some other troubling trends: The U.S. already has large local and regional disparities in educational funding, Minow noted, while schools have actually become significantly more segregated in economic and ethnic terms over the last three decades. 

In this context, AI threatens to further weaken independent-thinking skills, Minow suggested, just when greater understanding of civic issues is absolutely vital. 

“As AI surges, I think we have to learn to be smarter about how to use it, how to regulate it, and how to actually educate people about the costs of mindless using,” Minow said. She added: “Dominant AI platforms supercharge the strategies that are deployed by social media companies, inducing passivity in people … Leading AI models and interfaces and sycophantic elements endanger the development particularly of young people’s capabilities to think, to remember, and to engage in critical thinking.” 

That trend away from cognitive effort, she suggested, can be changed — perhaps through AI tools that act more like tutors and are designed to enhance people’s deep thinking.

“Existing LLMs, model training, and interface design can offer nudges and questions and hints rather than replacing student work, but there’s so much more that could be developed, and more effectively, to be trustworthy, and to deepen human activities and curiosity, rather than replacing people,” Minow said.

To the audience, she added, “AI tools could do much more of that … And I believe that you, the people here, could develop better tools than the ones that are out there. And make better assessments, more meaningful and cheating-resistant.” 

Minow’s talk, “Constituting Democracy in the Era of AI,” was delivered to a large audience in MIT’s Huntington Hall, Room 10-250 on campus.

MIT President Sally A. Kornbluth delivered introductory remarks to the audience. The Karl Taylor Compton Lecture Series, introduced in 1957, is the highest-profile event of its kind at MIT. Karl Taylor Compton was MIT’s ninth president, serving from 1930 to 1948, and then becoming chair of the MIT Corporation from 1948 to 1954.

“He guided MIT through the Great Depression and World War II,” Kornbluth said, “transforming the Institute from an outstanding school for training job-ready engineers to a great global research university.” 

She added: “He was also a deeply committed patriot who helped harness the intellectual power of America’s research universities to serve the nation during World War II.” 

Kornbluth called Minow “a legal scholar of extraordinary intellectual scope,” and a “dedicated educator whose work has shaped how we think about the law and our own humanity, as individuals and as a society.” 

Minow has been a faculty member at Harvard Law School since 1981, and served as dean of the school from 2009 through 2017. Minow earned her BA in history from the University of Michigan, an MA in education from Harvard, and a JD from Yale University.

Minow’s books include “Making All the Difference” (1990), “Partners Not Rivals” (2002), and “When Should Law Forgive?” (2020). 

In her talk, Minow also discussed the civic effects of misinformation, threats of violence, and multiple dimension of societal fairness. Modern media technology has led to a 75 percent reduction in journalists in recent decades, Minow observed, with an attendant rise in corruption in places without local media. Civic-minded technologists, she proposed, should work towards establishing a widely-used “information commons,” or many forms of them, to help people access more reliable information. 

Meanwhile, when it comes to basic security in society, Minow warned, “We’re on the brink right now. I know a lot of judges, and every one of them has a credible threat of violence against them. In America. This is not acceptable.” 

For all the challenges to democracy and traditional civic norms, however, Minow sounded positive notes throughout her remarks, pointing out that there are many opportunities to create new forms of reliable information, education, and community relations. 

“We have to actually invent the world that we want to live in,” she offered. 

Minow’s remarks were followed by a Q&A session in which Kornbluth read aloud questions submitted by the audience — and asked her to characterize her concerns about present trends. 

“I worry about the loss of the Enlightenment,” Minow said. “I worry about the loss of the belief that reason, and testing hypotheses, and rejecting myths in the face of evidence, and the toleration and rights and expansion of participation that came along with the Enlightenment, that’s what concerns me the most. That’s why the disinformation issue for me is so important, that’s why the loss of critical thinking in schools is so important.”

She added: “I’ve spent much of my own career thinking about mass violence. What happens when people don’t understand each other, and are afraid. And it’s terrible, and we don’t want to be there. And I do view the Enlightenment as a time when people learned that actually having mass wars is a bad thing, and coming up with toleration is a good thing, and testing our ideas in light of evidence other people can share can produce a better life for everybody. I worry we’re abandoning that right now.”

items.title: Highlights from Garrison Lovely's "Obsolete"
items.content:
I’ve just finished reading Garrison Lovely’s recently released book, “Obsolete.” I wish I had time for a longer review, but I’ll give a brief one and highlight some particularly interesting sections below. I think it’s a great introduction to non-technical readers and even as a pretty dedicated reader of AI policy and news I learned a good bit. It’s deeply, deeply researched and has a good pulse on the alignment community, and Lovely is careful not to understate or overstate his case. The core argument is that AI development should be analyzed through the lens of mass or universal labor displacement, and that a mass movement to shape, pause or freeze development is much more possible, much more positive, and capable of greater breadth of salience and support than is often argued in the alignment community.

He makes an, in my opinion, decisive case that “competitive pressures” by themselves don’t dictate that AI development is fated to happen, and certainly not that it’s fated to happen at the pace the frontier labs are setting. But I wish he’d been a bit more careful about the limitations and subtleties of the plan he’s advocating for; I share the concern raised by folks like the AIFP that it’s hard to pause indefinitely at any given point for very long and that the cost to train a model at any fixed intelligence level, once first reached, is falling precipitously, and that many well-capitalized actors currently want to and are able to speed up development precipitously. I think the book somewhat elides the difficulties we’d still have even if this number were close to 0....

items.title: The Evil is where you aren’t looking
items.content:
We have a tendency to judge past societies more harshly than our own. That is partly because we tend to focus on the evils of past societies that many people at the time either weren’t aware of, or didn’t spend much time thinking about.

Most Germans claimed to be unaware of the extent of Nazi war crimes until they were revealed after the war ended. Few Britons were aware of the brutality of the slave trade until Thomas Clarkson’s anti slavery investigations of the 18th century. During the colonial period, most Europeans were unaware of the extent of the abuses inflicted on indigenous people. Few people were aware of the abuses that took place in large scale psychiatric institutions in the 1950s.

Some people argue that our current society will be judged harshly by future generations for the way it treats factory farmed animals - which is something that a lot of people are somewhat aware of but spend little time thinking about.

I suspect that our society, like all past societies, will be judged more harshly than we expect, and that much of what future generations will condemn us for will either be things we are unaware of, or spend little time thinking about. While we shouldn’t ignore the evils of the past, we should do so with humility, because we are probably messing up more than we realize too.

items.title: Is Gaming the Future of Humanity?
items.content:
One hot topic of conversation right now is “What are all the humans going to do when AI plus humanoid robotics becomes better at everything?”.

As William Gibson famously said “The future is already here — it’s just not very evenly distributed”. So it’s worth looking at what activities are already taking up excess human time, allowing humans to form status hierarchies, and satisfying the human need to feel like they are accomplishing something.

One of those activities is video games, which continue to take up an increasing fraction of people’s time. But many other human activities can in some senses be seen as being forms of gaming - in the sense that they are activities that lead to dubious material benefits, but allow people to gain status and feel accomplished. This includes a large fraction of academia (definitely not all), the art world, sports, and yes, blogging.

Some people even believe superintelligence actually happened a long time ago, and what we experience now is actually a simulated video game reality, designed to keep us entertained.

items.title: Reinforcing the value of human understanding at MIT
items.content:
At the MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS) 75th Anniversary Symposium, speakers celebrated the school’s value and contributions, while exploring how artificial intelligence is transforming many aspects of teaching, research, and society.

The symposium was held Sept. 24-25 in the Linde Music Building’s Thomas Tull Concert Hall. Scholars, students, staff, and alumni from across SHASS and MIT gathered for the event, which kicked off with welcoming remarks from MIT leadership. 

“How should we think about MIT’s School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences? With enthusiastic appreciation and gratitude,” said President Sally Kornbluth.

The school’s origins date back to the Lewis Committee Report, commissioned by MIT and published in 1949, which called for stronger integration between scientific and technical topics and humanistic scholarship and teaching.

Kornbluth noted that, much like when the school was founded just after World War II, the world faces uncertainty as it grapples with the broad implications of artificial intelligence.

“AI has suddenly arrived with enormous consequences for both research and education,” she said. “As we face the challenges of our own time, and our own society, it’s clear that MIT has never needed your particular insight and guidance more than we do now.”

In opening remarks, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan described the importance of a human-centered approach to technology, one that considers both its efficacy and its impacts. He lauded many of the new research projects happening through the MIT Human Insight Collaborative, a strategic initiative launched in 2024.

“Today — a time of rapid, AI-driven change — the arts, humanities, and social sciences are as important as ever,” he said. “To be able to contribute effectively to solving the world’s great challenges, it is not enough to gain technical mastery.”

Chancellor Melissa Nobles recalled how, during her tenure as SHASS dean from 2015 to 2021, reading the positive feedback from students in their SHASS course assessments reinforced the value of the school’s teaching.

“MIT students have a range of interests that draw them to our classes that may be invisible to their STEM professors, but that we very well know our students have,” said Nobles, who is also a professor of political science.

Agustín Rayo, the Kenan Sahin Dean of SHASS and professor of philosophy, noted that, while research in the school plays a key role in addressing global issues such as climate change and AI, the value of the work in SHASS should not be measured by practical application alone.

“Education should also help us ask what is worth doing, what do we owe one another, and what makes a life worth living,” Rayo said. “Some research matters because it helps us understand the histories, cultures, and social structures that have made us who we are. Some things matter because they enrich human life.”

Scholarship from across SHASS and beyond 

Over the symposium’s two days, research presentations, panel discussions, and performances offered attendees opportunities to engage with the role of SHASS in exploring today’s biggest societal questions.

“We gather not so much to look back over the past 75 years, but to showcase where we are now, and share what we urgently aim to tackle together in the years ahead,” said David Kaiser, Germeshausen Professor of the History of Science and professor of physics at MIT, who also served as chair of the symposium planning committee.

The first day included a session on teaching and learning innovations. Faculty presented on the success of educational programs housed within SHASS, including the MIT Indigenous Languages Initiative Master's Program, the Master in Data, Economics, and Design of Policy (DEDP), and MISTI, the hub for global experiences for MIT students.

Stephanie Seed, associate professor of literature, spoke about why she and others are working to reintegrate classic books into their teaching.

“MIT, of course, is an institution unusually oriented towards the future,” she said. “Our students are trained to imagine and create worlds that don’t yet exist. And it’s precisely this future orientation that makes reading the past especially important here.”

Eric Klopfer, professor of Comparative Media Studies/Writing and co-author of MIT’s recent report on AI and instruction, said this is a moment when instructors must reassess how courses are taught.

“I don’t know exactly what that looks like, but I do think it means something that’s more than modifying our curriculum. I think it really means rethinking what the educational experience is,” he said.

The first day concluded with a rousing Music and Theater Arts performance showcase, which began with an excerpt from Stan Lai’s “A Dream Like A Dream,” a play directed and performed by students and instructors in class 21T.100 (Theater Arts Production).

“I’ve attended every session, and this is a fantastic program and a great celebration of the 75th anniversary,” he said. “Clearly, whether it’s AI impact, the impact of climate change, or the impact of political and social change, SHASS is in the right place at the right time.”

At the MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS) 75th Anniversary Symposium, speakers celebrated the school’s value and contributions, while exploring how artificial intelligence is transforming many aspects of teaching, research, and society.

The symposium was held Sept. 24-25 in the Linde Music Building’s Thomas Tull Concert Hall. Scholars, students, staff, and alumni from across SHASS and MIT gathered for the event, which kicked off with welcoming remarks from MIT leadership.

“How should we think about MIT’s School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences? With enthusiastic appreciation and gratitude,” said President Sally Kornbluth.

The school’s origins date back to the Lewis Committee Report, commissioned by MIT and published in 1949, which called for stronger integration between scientific and technical topics and humanistic scholarship and teaching.

Kornbluth noted that, much like when the school was founded just after World War II, the world faces uncertainty as it grapples with the broad implications of artificial intelligence.

items.title: How to Handle the Demise of Every Human Talent?
items.content:
Context: AI can now program, draw, animate, create music, do math, write, and probably many more things, almost equally/equally/better than most/all humans, and at scale. Probably, soon it will close the last gaps.

Since I was young, I wanted to "leave my mark on the world". It didn't have to be a big mark - or maybe it did - but whatever. I wanted to create, or discover, something, that will be remembered or used long after I'm gone (e.g. Olympic athletes, social people, and murderers do leave some kind of impact on the world, but it wasn't what I wanted). I learned to program at around 10, I started doing my first degree (computer science) at 13, and now (early twenties) I'm doing my PhD, in... AI.

I do have some achievements I'm proud of. Around 14, I created some multiplayer video games that went somewhat popular in my school, and people literally played it quite often, around 5-10 people together (we had a lab in the school and it was forbidden to play games there, however they "only helped me debug my game"). I left this school at some point, however I continued to program games until about 18, and am still proud of each, even the ones no one besides me played.

I invited a stupid fake religion that went somewhat known/discussed in my (religious) school's year group too, that was also something.

Meanwhile, I become interested in AI (a bit before gpt2, I think). After finishing my first degree, and working a bit, I started doing my masters, and then continued to PhD. I published a few papers, some on game theory (somehow in the academy it's considered AI and is published in AI conferences), some on interpretability (not because I was concerned about AI safety, I just found it interesting). One paper got some tenth of citations and I'm also somewhat proud of it....
